item.title: Hasan Nawaz's fighting 96 against India in vain as Pakistan settle for Asian Games cricket silver. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Hasan Nawaz’s fighting 96 went in vain as Pakistan fell 19 runs short of India’s 212-run target to settle for silver in the Asian Games men’s cricket final at the Korogi Athletic Park in Nisshin, Japan on Saturday.

Hasan struck five fours and seven sixes in his 51-ball innings before being caught behind off Shivam Dube from the final ball of the match, with Pakistan finishing on 192 for six.

Needing 33 from the last over after reaching 179 for five, Pakistan kept their hopes alive when Hasan hit Dube for a boundary and then a six. But a yorker from the India all-rounder followed by two dot balls left Hasan needing four for his century from the final delivery.

He attempted to clear the infield but was caught by wicket-keeper Sanju Samson, ending an innings that had briefly brought Pakistan back into contention.

Hasan’s dismissal completed a remarkable recovery after Pakistan had been 39 for three after six overs. He and Saim Ayub put on 87 for the fourth wicket before Saim was dismissed for 29 off 22 balls in the 15th over.

Hasan had reached his half-century from 28 balls and continued to attack India’s spinners, particularly Ravi Bishnoi, who conceded 44 from his three overs.

Pakistan were 126 for three after 14 overs, requiring 86 from the last 36 balls, but Dube removed Saim and Abdul Samad in successive stages of the closing overs to keep India ahead.

Saim was caught by Washington Sundar at square leg for 29 after attempting to use Dube’s pace, while Samad made nine before being caught by Tilak Varma off Washington in the 18th over.

Despite those setbacks, Hasan continued the assault. He reached 68 from 36 balls after hitting Axar Patel for a six in the 16th over and then struck two fours in Dube’s next over, one of them coming through an edge after he flashed at a short, wide delivery.

Pakistan reached 160 for four after 17 overs, needing 52 from the final 18 balls.

Saad Masood kept the chase alive with two sixes in his unbeaten 12 off five balls, but Bumrah’s fourth over yielded only 11 runs, leaving Pakistan 33 short with six balls remaining.

Dube was given the final over and conceded a boundary and a six to Hasan, but his yorkers at the crucial moment denied Pakistan the chance to complete the chase.

India’s bowlers had earlier kept Pakistan under pressure after the batters had posted 211 for six.

Pakistan’s chase had begun brightly enough but lost momentum after Sahibzada Farhan and Usman Khan departed in successive overs.

Farhan made 10 off 11 balls before attempting a slog-sweep against Sundar and finding Patel at deep midwicket. Usman followed for three off six, slogging a fuller delivery from Patel to Dube at midwicket.

Maaz Sadaqat, who made 23 off 18 balls with three fours, was then caught by Sundar off Patel at the start of the seventh over to leave Pakistan 39 for three.

Hasan and Saim rebuilt the innings, taking Pakistan to 76 for three at the halfway stage. Hasan was then 26 off 18 and Ayub 12 off nine.

The pair accelerated through the middle overs, with Hasan reaching his half-century from 28 balls. Their 87-run partnership gave Pakistan a realistic chance of chasing India’s imposing total, but Dube’s dismissal of Saim at 126 proved a significant turning point.

Varma stars

India had earlier been propelled to 211 for six by Varma and Dube, who added 62 from 31 balls for the sixth wicket.

Varma remained unbeaten on 51 off 22 balls, striking three fours and four sixes, while Dube made 27 off 15 with two fours and two sixes.

India had lost three wickets between the eighth and 15th overs after making an explosive start, but the late partnership lifted them beyond 200.

Abhishek Sharma provided the initial impetus with 61 off 28 balls, hitting three fours and seven sixes. Vaibhav Sooryavanshi made 15 off nine before being caught by Usman off Saim, while Sanju Samson was dismissed for two by Ahmed Daniyal.

Shreyas Iyer made 21 off 24 balls and Ishan Kishan 20 off 18. Ishan fell to Arafat Minhas at 128, while Iyer was dismissed by Abrar Ahmed five runs later.

India reached 114 in the first 10 overs before adding 97 in the second half of the innings. Varma reached his half-century from 21 balls and remained unbeaten, while Dube was dismissed by Daniyal in the first ball of the final over.

For Pakistan, Arafat took two for 25 from three overs and Daniyal two for 43. Abrar took one for 29 and Saim one for 47. Saad and Sufyan Moqim went wicketless.

Sri Lanka took the bronze medal after beating Bangladesh by 63 runs in the third-place playoff.

item.title: Democracy cannot survive with a fearful press. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
That at least 162 journalists across the country faced attacks, threats, and legal harassment in 112 separate incidents over the past three months while performing their professional duties, according to a monitoring report by private research organization Media Initiative for Development (MID), should alarm us.
When members of the media are systematically targeted simply for documenting public events, investigating corruption, or asking uncomfortable questions, it signals a dangerous erosion of basic rights.
A nation striving to rebuild its democratic institutions cannot succeed while those tasked with holding power accountable operate under constant fear for their safety.
In any functioning democracy, an independent press serves as the eyes and ears of the public, tasked with providing citizens with the objective facts necessary to make informed decisions.
When media workers are assaulted by political cadres, intimidated by influential interest groups, or subjected to arbitrary legal harassment, it is not merely an attack on individual reporters but a direct assault on the public's right to know.
This hostility toward journalism reflects a deep-seated, systemic culture of intolerance that has unfortunately persisted across political transitions, and has only been exacerbated as a result of the technology-enabled society we live in today.
When law enforcement agencies fail to protect working journalists on the ground or, worse, turn a blind eye to political mobs targeting newsrooms, it creates a chilling effect that fosters self-censorship.
It goes without saying that a media environment gripped by fear cannot fulfill its democratic mandate. Protecting press freedom requires more than public declarations but rather demands physical security, legal safeguards, and an environment where journalists can report without fear of retribution.
Democracy cannot survive without truth, and truth cannot surface when the press is silenced.

item.title: Revenue generation needs long-term planning. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The International Monetary Fund’s critical assessment of the National Board of Revenue’s (NBR) latest reform roadmap exposes a fundamental truth that has been an issue for Bangladesh for years: Short term, superficial administrative adjustments cannot resolve our chronic fiscal woes.
Despite repeated pledges to modernize tax collection and broaden the revenue base, it is disappointing that the NBR remains crippled by structural loopholes, slow execution, and a reliance on ad-hoc targets.
For a country maintaining one of the lowest tax-to-GDP ratios in South Asia , hovering under 8%, we must stop treating tax reform as a bureaucratic compliance exercise rather than the national priority it is.
The IMF’s critique rightly targets the core flaws of our revenue architecture. Rather than pursuing systemic modernization through comprehensive digitization, structural decoupling of tax policy from enforcement, and the elimination of discretionary exemptions, the revenue authority routinely defaults to squeezing existing taxpayers.
Setting ambitious revenue targets without fixing systemic leakages or curbing widespread tax evasion yields predictable shortfalls year after year. Furthermore, the persistent delay in fully automating tax administration and streamlining VAT collection perpetuates an environment ripe for rent-seeking and corruption.
Bangladesh can no longer afford an inefficient revenue apparatus. With growing debt-servicing obligations, rising social spending needs, and critical infrastructure demands, sustainable fiscal health depends on a modern, equitable, and transparent tax system.
As such, we hope and expect those at NBR to recognize that we learn to plan for the long term. For that to happen, we must start focusing on high-income earners and corporate entities currently operating outside official channels, rather than overburdening compliant businesses and middle-class citizens through indirect taxation.
Real reform requires genuine political will, not administrative posturing to satisfy multilateral lenders. Until the government replaces half-hearted measures with deep, structural reform, our fiscal stability will remain shaky.

item.title: India-Pakistan blockbuster brings cricket fever to Japan baseball field. [ dawn ]
item.description:
One of sport’s fiercest rivalries descended on a sleepy corner of Japan on Saturday as India and Pakistan clashed in the men’s cricket final at the Asian Games on a converted baseball field.

The neighbours only meet in international tournaments because of long-running political tensions and matches between them typically attract television audiences of hundreds of millions back home.

The gold-medal encounter in a suburban park in Nagoya was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for Indians and Pakistanis living in Japan.

They lined up hours before the game to get into the cosy 2,500-capacity purpose-built Korogi Athletic Park Stadium.

“I think this is never going to happen again, India against Pakistan in Japan,” long-time Nagoya resident Umer Dar, draped in a Pakistan flag, told AFP.

“I’m crazy about cricket but I never have the opportunity to watch it live because I’ve lived here for 26 years.”

The last time India and Pakistan collided was at the T20 World Cup in February, where they played in front of a sell-out 35,000 crowd in Sri Lanka.

The Asian Games setting was significantly more modest, with trees and a baseball pitcher’s mound just beyond the boundary.

The atmosphere was as passionate as ever though, with fans waving flags and cheering every ball from the temporary stands.

“We bought tickets three months back when they started selling them,” said Tokyo resident and India supporter Mohammed Kashim Raja.

“At the time it was easy but it became really difficult for others to get them.

“We heard that many people were selling them for high prices.”

Cricket is a niche sport in Japan and neutrals at the final appeared to be virtually non-existent.

‘Always crazy’

There was more of a casual crowd at the bronze-medal match between Sri Lanka and Bangladesh earlier, on a warm and sunny day.

Teachers Hiromi Niwa and Miki Kaede, both from nearby Gifu, said they knew nothing about cricket and had bought tickets out of curiosity.

After reading a free leaflet explaining the rules and watching some of the action, Kaede said it had been a “really fun” experience.

She was disappointed that their tickets did not get them into the final.

“We didn’t realise that India against Pakistan was such a big deal until we actually searched for it,” she said.

Cricket has a growing presence in Japan and the sport got a huge boost when India played their first-ever T20 international against Japan last week.

The historic match, celebrating 75 years of diplomatic relations, took place at Japan’s modest Sano International Cricket Ground outside Tokyo.

It was Japan’s first T20 game against a full-member nation, and they gave India a huge fright before losing by two runs in a rain-shortened match.

Kushal Gowda, an Indian fan living in Tokyo, said Japanese people were “trying to understand” cricket.

“We were trying to explain to our colleagues in our office and they were curious and keen to know what it was about,” he said.

“They kind of compared it with baseball.”

The crowd for the Asian Games final was overwhelmingly supporting India, with only a few Pakistan flags and shirts dotted around the ground.

A cheer went up when the gates opened to let fans in, and the party continued when the game began under clear skies.

“Even if it’s in Japan, the craze of India versus Pakistan is always there,” said Tokyo-based India fan Afroz Khan.

“Anywhere they play in the world, it’s always crazy.”

item.title: Universal registration key to sustainable health system and development. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Civil registration, specifically birth and death registration, serves as a primary legal identity of a citizen. Without these essential credentials, an individual remains practically invisible to the state, left to navigate a maze of systemic hurdles to access basic rights and public services.
In Bangladesh, however, nearly half the population exists outside this official framework. The national registration rates stand at a dismal 50% for births and 47% for deaths, lagging drastically behind regional and global averages.
This structural gap produces far-reaching consequences. A missing birth record means a child is absent from the central database, impairing national planning at its root. Without accurate demographic figures, health planners must operate blindfolded, unable to project precise vaccine quotas, identify areas with severe childhood malnutrition, or allocate pediatric specialists where they are most desperately needed.
Similarly, the absence of death registration dismantles the core health system of a nation. As public health experts emphasize, basic mortality data such as information about age, location, and causes of death functions as a nation's epidemiological compass. Lack of clear data on where non-communicable diseases like cardiovascular conditions, strokes, cancer, and diabetes strike hardest may misdirect millions of public funds into ineffective health infrastructure.
Real-time data forms an essential part of disease surveillance. Consider a scenario where several people in a remote village succumb to an unidentified fever. If these deaths are neither registered promptly nor assigned a cause, central authorities remain oblivious to an emerging viral outbreak. By the time news reaches the health ministry, a localized cluster may have already proliferated into an epidemic.
Furthermore, when crisis hits and life-saving vaccines or drugs must be distributed, unregistered, marginalized populations are systematically overlooked. Without a comprehensive database, any strategy to contain an epidemic is inherently flawed.
As a frontline victim of climate change, Bangladesh faces recurring cyclones, storm surges, and seasonal floods that routinely devastate its coastal margins. In the wake of a disaster, search-and-rescue teams face a critical question. How many are truly missing or dead? Without accurate local birth and death registries at the Union Parishad level, relief distribution and state rehabilitation funds quickly go astray.
Severe consequence occurs within the social safety net system. Failing to update death records in real time creates phantom beneficiaries on state rosters, while vulnerable women are often denied widow allowances because they lack an official death certificate for their deceased spouses. Consequently, the most impoverished and disaster-affected citizens are stripped of their basic state entitlements.
As a result, a question arises: Why does public participation in civil registration remain so sluggish? The answer lies in the structural loopholes of the Birth and Death Registration Act, 2004, compounded by bureaucratic complexities.
According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), 67% of births now occur within healthcare facilities. Yet, existing law places no direct mandate on hospital authorities to execute registrations. Instead, parents are forced to undertake an arduous visit to Union Parishad or City Corporation offices, where they routinely encounter technical glitches on online portals, tedious error-correction procedures, and informal fee extortion. Discouraged, thousands walk away, leaving their children legally invisible.
Target 16.9 of the Sustainable Development Goals envisions universal legal identity for all by 2030. Time is running short, and Bangladesh remains significantly off track. Closing this gap requires urgent legal amendment. The Birth and Death Registration Act, 2004 must be revised to shift the legal obligation of recording births and deaths directly onto health facilities, ensuring every newborn is registered at birth.
Across the Asia-Pacific, nations that transferred this administrative duty from individuals to healthcare institutions have successfully achieved universal civil registration.
Parallel to legal reform, technological issues must be resolved. Civil registration must be promoted as a fundamental human right. Tackling field-level staffing shortages, upgrading registrar training, and enforcing institutional accountability are non-negotiable steps toward a functional system.
Civil registration is far more than a routine ledger or a string of digital digits. It is the structural backbone of resilient public health, sustainable development, and crisis management.
The choice before us is evident. Do we continue allowing millions of citizens to remain invisible, anchoring our future to an unreliable, data-starved system? Or do we leverage targeted legal reform and modern technology to build a secure, inclusive, and resilient Bangladesh by 2030? The time to act is now.
Mashiat Abedin is Coordinator, and ABM Zubair is Executive Director, PROGGA (Knowledge for Progress).

item.title: The new power that shapes the world. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Wars have traditionally been decided by soldiers, weapons, and economic strength. But the character of power is changing rapidly. In the modern world, information technology and communication have become strategic weapons as powerful as missiles, aircraft, or financial resources. The recent Iran conflict has demonstrated this reality with extraordinary clarity.
The most important question in a modern conflict is no longer simply who has more weapons. It is increasingly who knows more, who knows it faster, and who can communicate it more effectively.
Modern military operations have depended heavily on satellite imagery, electronic surveillance, artificial intelligence, drones, radar systems, cyber capabilities, and real-time communications. The United States has acknowledged striking Iranian radar, air-defense, maritime, and communications facilities -- illustrating how information and communication networks themselves have become critical strategic targets.
US officials have linked high-resolution satellite imagery obtained by Iran to improved targeting capabilities in attacks against American military facilities. Whatever the political controversy surrounding the allegation, the episode demonstrates one fundamental reality: Accurate information can dramatically increase the effectiveness of military power.
The lesson is even clearer in Ukraine. Satellite communication has become an essential part of battlefield operations. Starlink-based communications have been used to coordinate forces and drones, while Russia has attempted to disrupt the system through electronic warfare. Reuters reported in July 2026 that Russian forces were trying to jam Starlink to counter Ukrainian drone operations.
The battlefield is no longer confined to land, sea, and air. There is now a fourth battlefield -- the information and communication domain.
But technology alone cannot win every conflict. Information becomes meaningful only when human beings can interpret it correctly and communicate intelligently.
This brings us to the second great power of the modern age: Communication.
A crisis may begin with weapons, economic pressure, or political disagreement, but it can often be contained through communication. A telephone call between leaders, a diplomatic message, a trusted intermediary, or a carefully negotiated agreement can prevent a conflict from becoming a catastrophe.
The Iran crisis itself illustrates this paradox. Despite military confrontation, diplomatic channels have repeatedly remained important.
Even in September 2026, diplomacy remains central to managing the consequences of the conflict. Iran and the United Arab Emirates endorsed a BRICS statement calling for restraint, protection of civilians and safeguarding global trade and maritime stability.
Another contemporary example comes from Ukraine. Recent US-backed diplomatic efforts have brought Russian and Ukrainian representatives into renewed discussions concerning possible peace arrangements, energy infrastructure, grain shipments, and prisoner exchanges. No final settlement has emerged, but the process demonstrates that communication remains indispensable even when military confrontation continues.
The same principle applies outside warfare. In business, the company with the best product does not necessarily become the market leader. The winner is often the company that understands its customers fastest, uses data intelligently, and communicates its value most effectively.
In healthcare, information technology enables doctors to access medical records, diagnostic images, and specialist advice rapidly. In education, digital communication allows knowledge to cross geographical boundaries. In agriculture, farmers can receive weather, market, and crop information through mobile networks. In disaster management, early warnings communicated through digital platforms can save thousands of lives.
Artificial intelligence is now accelerating this transformation. It can analyze enormous amounts of information, identify patterns, and support decision-making within seconds. Recent reporting has even shown how AI can be exploited to collect information about military vessels, analyze satellite imagery, and conduct influence operations.
This creates both opportunity and danger.
The same technology that can save lives can also spread misinformation. The same communication network that connects families can be used for propaganda, manipulation, and cyberattacks. The same artificial intelligence that helps doctors can potentially assist criminals or hostile actors.
Therefore, technological power without ethical responsibility can become dangerous.
For developing countries such as Bangladesh, this global transformation offers an enormous opportunity. Bangladesh should not view information technology merely as a tool for social media or outsourcing. It should be treated as a national strategic asset.
The country needs stronger investment in cybersecurity, satellite technology, digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence, data science, and advanced communication systems.
Bangladesh needs a culture of intelligent communication. Political disagreement, business disputes, diplomatic tensions and social conflicts cannot always be solved through confrontation. Sometimes the most powerful weapon is a well-timed conversation.
The world is entering an era in which information moves at the speed of light, technology converts information into power, and communication determines how that power is used.
The Iran war has shown that knowing the battlefield can be as important as controlling it. Ukraine has demonstrated the strategic importance of secure communication. Contemporary diplomacy has shown that even after missiles are launched, communication remains the pathway toward de-escalation.
The lesson for the 21st century is therefore simple but profound: Weapons may win battles, but information shapes the battlefield -- and communication can determine whether the next battle happens at all.
For nations, institutions and individuals alike, the future will belong not simply to those who possess the most technology, but to those who can collect information intelligently, understand it accurately, and communicate it wisely.
Md Sultan Uddin is a banker.

item.title: Ensuring exports stay on the up. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh’s export performance in the first quarter of FY27 offers a welcome sign of resilience, especially at a time when the economy continues to face a range of challenges.
According to reports, merchandise exports rose by 6.34% year-on-year to $13.09 billion between July and September, while September alone recorded an 8.54% growth.
The continued strength of the readymade garment sector is also particularly encouraging. RMG exports grew 6.10% during the quarter to $10.58b, with both knitwear and woven garments recording solid growth.
This remains an important source of foreign exchange and employment, and its performance demonstrates the continued competitiveness of Bangladeshi exporters in global markets.
More encouraging still is the performance of several non-RMG sectors. Pharmaceutical exports grew 40.39%, while jute and jute goods rose 31.55%, leather and leather products 14.74%, and light engineering 16.51%.
These figures are proof that Bangladesh has considerable potential beyond its traditional dependence on garments.
However, this progress should be treated as an opportunity to build on rather than a reason for complacency. Agricultural products and frozen and live fish recorded negative growth, showing that important areas of the export basket still require attention.
Greater diversification will be essential if Bangladesh is to make its export earnings more resilient to changes in global demand.
The government must therefore focus on removing the structural obstacles that continue to affect exporters, including energy shortages, high production costs, logistical bottlenecks, and bureaucratic delays.
Support for product upgrading, market expansion, and trade facilitation must translate into practical measures that businesses can actually benefit from.
The latest figures are undoubtedly positive: They reflect the efforts of exporters and workers and the continued demand for Bangladeshi products.
Now, the priority should be to sustain this momentum, strengthen emerging sectors, and open more markets so that export growth becomes broader, more stable, and capable of supporting Bangladesh’s long-term economic ambitions.

item.title: Small businesses need more support. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The newly announced requirement making a Business Identification Number (BIN) mandatory for opening or operating business bank accounts and accessing loans has created serious difficulties for micro, small, and medium enterprises (CMSMEs).
While the objective of widening the tax and VAT net is understandable, its implementation must not undermine the very businesses that generate employment and drive economic activity.
Bangladesh needs more businesses to enter the formal economy, but this cannot happen if the process of becoming formal itself becomes a barrier to doing business.
Bangladesh has around 11.7 million economic units, nearly 99% of which are CMSMEs. Together, they employ more than 30 million people and contribute an estimated 25-32% of GDP. These businesses therefore cannot be treated as an administrative afterthought.
When entrepreneurs struggle to obtain the necessary documentation for a BIN, and consequently face delays in opening accounts or securing credit, the effects extend well beyond individual businesses.
The Association of Bankers, Bangladesh has already urged the National Board of Revenue to exempt micro, cottage, and small businesses or introduce a phased approach. The NBR, however, has said the requirement is mandated by law and cannot simply be waived.
This is precisely why the focus should now be on making compliance easier. If formalization is the goal, registration procedures should be simplified, documentation requirements reduced, services made genuinely accessible online, and adequate transition time provided.
Banks and relevant agencies should also coordinate so that entrepreneurs are not forced to navigate multiple layers of bureaucracy.
While revenue mobilization is important, creating an environment in which businesses can start, survive, and expand is equally necessary. Bangladesh needs more entrepreneurship, investment, and employment -- not more red tape.
The principle should be straightforward: Compliance must be encouraged, but doing business must be made easier. A stronger formal economy will only emerge from removing unnecessary obstacles instead of adding new ones.
